mcqs.q: When injected into soft tissue, most local anaesthetics produce:
mcqs.explain: Injected LAs cause vasodilation, which is why vasoconstrictors are usually added.

mcqs.q: Which local anaesthetic is the most potent vasodilator?
mcqs.explain: Procaine is the most potent vasodilator among local anaesthetics; cocaine is the exception that vasoconstricts.

mcqs.q: The only local anaesthetic that consistently produces vasoconstriction is:
mcqs.explain: Cocaine is the only LA that consistently produces vasoconstriction; all others vasodilate.

mcqs.q: A clinically important consequence of LA-induced vasodilation is:
opts: Faster absorption into blood → shorter, less profound anaesthesia and higher toxicity risk
mcqs.explain: Vasodilation speeds absorption, shortening and weakening anaesthesia while raising blood levels and overdose risk.

mcqs.q: After oral administration, lidocaine is largely inactivated by:
mcqs.explain: Most LAs (especially lidocaine) are poorly absorbed orally and undergo a significant hepatic first-pass effect.

mcqs.q: Topical LA absorption is almost as rapid as intravenous when applied to the:
mcqs.explain: Tracheal mucosal absorption is nearly as rapid as IV; pharyngeal absorption is slower and intact skin gives no effect.

mcqs.q: EMLA cream is used to anaesthetise intact skin and contains:
mcqs.explain: EMLA (eutectic mixture) is lidocaine 2.5% + prilocaine 2.5%, applied about 1 hour before the procedure because intact skin is a diffusion barrier.

mcqs.q: Which route gives the most rapid elevation of LA blood levels?
mcqs.explain: IV administration provides the fastest rise in blood levels and is used clinically to manage ventricular dysrhythmias.

mcqs.q: Which tissue contains the greatest total percentage of local anaesthetic in the body?
mcqs.explain: Although highly perfused organs reach high levels first, skeletal muscle holds the greatest total amount because of its large mass.

mcqs.q: Ester local anaesthetics are metabolised by:
mcqs.explain: Esters are hydrolysed in plasma by pseudocholinesterase; amides are metabolised in the liver.

mcqs.q: Allergic reactions to ester local anaesthetics are usually caused by:
mcqs.explain: Ester allergy is usually due to PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid), a major metabolite, not the parent compound.

mcqs.q: A patient with atypical (hereditary) pseudocholinesterase is at risk because they:
opts: Cannot hydrolyse ester LAs, leading to prolonged high levels and toxicity
Are immune to all local anaesthetics
mcqs.explain: Atypical pseudocholinesterase (~1 in 2800) cannot hydrolyse esters, prolonging high blood levels and increasing toxicity — a contraindication.

mcqs.q: Amide local anaesthetics are biotransformed primarily in the:
mcqs.explain: The liver is the primary site of amide biotransformation; articaine is metabolised in both blood and liver.

mcqs.q: Why are amide LAs a relative contraindication in cirrhosis or congestive heart failure?
opts: Reduced hepatic metabolism raises blood levels and toxicity risk
They cannot bind the sodium channel
The liver destroys them too fast
They are excreted entirely by the lungs
mcqs.explain: Low hepatic blood flow or poor liver function slows amide biotransformation, raising blood levels and toxicity risk.

mcqs.q: The primary organ for excretion of LAs and their metabolites is the:
mcqs.explain: The kidneys are the primary excretory organ; amides appear in urine more than esters, which are largely hydrolysed in plasma.

mcqs.q: At toxic blood levels, the primary CNS manifestation of LA overdose is:
mcqs.explain: LAs cross the blood–brain barrier; at toxic levels the primary effect is a generalized tonic–clonic convulsion, later progressing to CNS depression.

mcqs.q: On the cardiovascular system, local anaesthetics:
opts: Decrease myocardial excitability, conduction rate and force of contraction
Have no cardiac effect at any dose
mcqs.explain: LAs depress the myocardium — decreasing excitability, conduction and contractility — which is used therapeutically as an anti-dysrhythmic, but in overdose causes circulatory collapse.

mcqs.q: Procaine has a slow clinical onset (6–10 minutes) mainly because of its:
mcqs.explain: Procaine's high pKa (9.1) leaves little uncharged base at pH 7.4, giving a slow onset of 6–10 minutes.

mcqs.q: The 'gold standard' local anaesthetic against which others are compared is:
mcqs.explain: Lidocaine (amide, rapid onset 3–5 min) is the gold standard for comparison; it has a potency reference of 1.

mcqs.q: The FDA maximum recommended dose of lidocaine (with or without vasoconstrictor) is:
mcqs.explain: Lidocaine's maximum is 7 mg/kg for adults and children, not to exceed an absolute 500 mg.

mcqs.q: Compared with lidocaine, mepivacaine is notable for:
opts: Only slight vasodilation (so it is used 3% without a vasoconstrictor)
mcqs.explain: Mepivacaine (potency 1) causes only slight vasodilation, so it can be used as a 3% plain solution (2% with a vasoconstrictor).

mcqs.q: A clinically useful property of articaine is that it:
opts: Diffuses well through tissues, so buccal infiltration may anaesthetise the palate
Has the lowest potency of all amides
mcqs.explain: Articaine (potency 1.5, metabolised in blood and liver) diffuses through hard and soft tissues well, so a maxillary buccal infiltration may provide palatal anaesthesia.

mcqs.q: Bupivacaine is chosen for long procedures and post-operative pain because it has:
opts: About 4× the potency of lidocaine and the longest duration
The fastest onset of all LAs
The shortest duration of all LAs
mcqs.explain: Bupivacaine is ~4× as potent as lidocaine with a long duration (pulpal 90–180 min, soft tissue 4–8 h), though its onset is slow.

mcqs.q: Bupivacaine is generally avoided in young children and disabled patients because of the risk of:
mcqs.explain: Its long soft-tissue anaesthesia increases the risk of self-inflicted lip/cheek/tongue injury in these groups.

mcqs.q: Topical local anaesthetics are effective only on surface tissue to a depth of about:
opts: The full thickness of the jaw
mcqs.explain: Topicals act only on surface tissues (2–3 mm), enough to allow atraumatic needle penetration; they use a higher concentration than injectables.

mcqs.q: Benzocaine is used only topically (not by injection) because it is:
opts: An ester with poor water solubility
mcqs.explain: Benzocaine is an ester with poor water solubility, unsuitable for injection; it is supplied as aerosol, gel or ointment.

mcqs.q: The elimination half-life of a local anaesthetic is the time for:
opts: A 50% reduction in its blood level
The drug to reach the brain
mcqs.explain: The elimination half-life is the time necessary for a 50% reduction in the blood level.

mcqs.q: On intact (undamaged) skin, topical local anaesthetics (other than EMLA):
opts: Provide no anaesthetic action, but relieve pain on sunburned skin
Are absorbed as fast as IV
mcqs.explain: Applied to intact skin they give no anaesthetic action, but on sun-damaged skin they bring rapid relief (sunburn ointments contain lidocaine/benzocaine).

mcqs.q: Among ester anaesthetics, which is hydrolysed most slowly and has the greatest toxic potential?
mcqs.explain: Chloroprocaine is hydrolysed fastest (least toxic); tetracaine is hydrolysed ~16× more slowly and has the greatest toxic potential.

saqs.q: Explain LA vasodilation and its clinical importance.
saqs.a: Injected LAs cause vasodilation (procaine most potent; cocaine the only vasoconstrictor). This speeds absorption, shortening and weakening anaesthesia and raising blood levels/overdose risk — hence vasoconstrictors are added.

saqs.q: Contrast the metabolism of ester and amide LAs.
saqs.a: Esters are hydrolysed in plasma by pseudocholinesterase (allergy via PABA). Amides are metabolised in the liver (articaine in blood + liver). The kidneys excrete both.

saqs.q: Describe the CNS and CVS effects of LA toxicity.
saqs.a: CNS: cross the blood–brain barrier → depression; toxic levels cause a generalized tonic–clonic convulsion, then cerebral depression. CVS: myocardial depression (↓excitability, conduction, contractility) → circulatory collapse and possibly death.

saqs.q: Why is anaesthesia in an infected area linked to procaine's slow onset?
saqs.a: Procaine has a high pKa (9.1), so little uncharged base exists at pH 7.4 → slow onset (6–10 min). Infected/acidic tissue further reduces the base form, worsening efficacy.

saqs.q: Give the key properties of lidocaine.
saqs.a: Amide, gold standard, 2% effective, pKa 7.9, rapid onset (3–5 min), liver metabolism, max dose 7 mg/kg (≤500 mg).

Articaine 4% — potency 1.5, metabolised in blood + liver, fast onset, diffuses to the palate after buccal infiltration. Bupivacaine 0.5% — 4× lidocaine potency, slow onset, longest duration; avoid in children/disabled (self-mutilation).

Higher concentration than injectables (to diffuse through mucosa, ↑toxicity), effective only on surface tissue (2–3 mm), allowing atraumatic needle penetration. Examples: benzocaine (ester, not injectable) and lidocaine (base 5%/soluble 2%, max 200 mg).
